# The Last Truly Shared Experience: Live Sports Own the Attention Economy

RF

Russell Fink Oct 2026· 3 min read

Mitch is a diehard New York Jets fan. He lives and breathes all things football. Throughout his life, Sundays in the fall were sacred; plans were moved and calls ignored because he was home watching the game.

Then he got married, had kids, and like most parents discovered that Sundays suddenly included birthday parties, youth sports, family obligations, and all the other things that apparently don't stop just because kickoff is at 1:00 PM.

So, he came up with a solution. He recorded the games in their entirety to watch later. But here was the catch: no one was allowed to talk Jets if they saw Mitch on a Sunday. He was on a total news blackout for the day. Each Sunday night, he would go home, put the kids to bed, give his wife a hug, and sit down to watch the game as if it were live.

But it wasn’t.

I asked him why it wasn’t the same, and he just shrugged and said, “It’s just not.” The same elements were there: the unknown, the uncertainty, and the excitement of what might happen next. Everything was theoretically identical, but it wasn't. Why? It came down to this:

He was alone.

### The Isolation of the Replay

Today, we have more content and more ways to consume it than at any point in history. The streaming wars, YouTube, social media, and podcasts have offered us unprecedented personalization and control. But there is a tradeoff. We have more ways to connect, yet we watch more individually. Along the way, we lost some of the simultaneity that creates a connected community.

There was a time when television brought huge portions of the country together. We watched the same shows at the same time and discussed them at the water cooler the next day. That is becoming rarer. Yes, Netflix can produce a massive hit like Squid Game, YouTube can generate hundreds of millions of views for MrBeast, and TikTok can shape how we dance and speak. These are incredible shared cultural experiences, but that is not the same as a simultaneous experience.

### Cultural Scale vs. Simultaneous Impact

Think about what we have seen in 2026. Super Bowl LX averaged over 125 million viewers. Nearly 63 million Americans watched the World Cup Final. The Milano Cortina Olympics averaged 24 million U.S. viewers, and approximately 21 million Americans watched the USA-Canada gold-medal hockey game—even more impressive given its 8:15 AM EST start time. Millions of people watch sports live, not just for the result, but for the shared experience.

And that is what Mitch was missing. When he used to watch the Jets live, he may have been physically alone, but he wasn’t isolated. Thousands of fellow fans and millions of NFL viewers were right there with him. When he recorded the game, he could recreate the action, but he couldn’t recreate the community.

### The Power of Belonging

There is a deep psychological driver behind this. In the famous Asch Conformity experiments, participants were asked to match line lengths. The answers were obvious, but actors in the room intentionally gave incorrect responses. Faced with a unanimous group saying something blatantly wrong, many participants went along with them anyway. Why? Because the desire to belong is extraordinarily powerful.

We want to belong to a group so much that it can cause us to trust the collective over our own eyes. Sports turns that group dynamic into a live experience. We cheer together, complain together, celebrate together, and suffer together. The community we create turns viewing into a simultaneous event.

In today’s attention economy, scarcity creates value, and few things are scarcer than simultaneity. Ratings, reach, advertising, and subscriptions still matter, but bringing a massive audience together at the exact same time is more valuable than ever.

Traditional entertainment can build massive audiences over days, weeks, or years—but sports brings those same crowds, often even larger ones, all at once. That explains why sports rights remain so valuable and why every platform wants a piece of the action. The value isn’t just reach; it is shared reach.

### The Streaming Contradiction

Yet here lies the central contradiction of modern media: as these shared experiences become more valuable, the industry continues to fragment them. Watching a single team can require multiple subscriptions and apps. The industry aggressively sells sports’ power to aggregate audiences while fragmenting those same viewers across platforms.

The rest of the media landscape encourages you to personalize your entertainment, news, and algorithm. Modern media is built around my content, my algorithm, my device, and my schedule. Sports remains one of the few places where " my" becomes " ours."

Live sports don't just give us something to watch. They give us something to experience together. Mitch could recreate the Jets game, but he couldn't recreate everyone watching it with him. In an entertainment world built on watching whatever we want, whenever we want, sports may be the last truly shared experience.
